tool_arguments.summary: Reconstruction of Proto-Tongic from Tongan and Niuean. Proto-Tongic preserves Proto-Polynesian *ʔ (retained in Tongan as ʔ and lost in Niuean), Proto-Tongic *t before *i (preserved in Niuean as t, spirantized to s in Tongan), Proto-Tongic *l in *lima (sporadically assimilated to n in Tongan), and the diphthong *au in *au and *lau (preserved in Niuean, rounded to ou in Tongan). Long vowels in Niuean fetuː and veː reflect regular vowel contraction/monophthongization following the loss of intervocalic *ʔ (*fetuʔu > fetuː, *vaʔe > veː). Niuean orthographic g corresponds to the velar nasal *ŋ.

anomalies.explanation: Tongan nima exhibits sporadic nasal assimilation of initial *l- to n- before the bilabial nasal -m-, whereas Niuean lima and Polynesian outgroups preserve original Proto-Tongic *lima.
Tongan ʔelelo exhibits sporadic anticipatory vowel assimilation of *a to e before the following -e-, whereas Niuean alelo and all Polynesian outgroups preserve Proto-Tongic *ʔalelo.
Tongan fefine and Niuean fifine show divergent vowel raising of the initial syllable relative to Proto-Polynesian *fafine.
Lexical divergence in the word for father: Tongan reflects PTong *tamai, whereas Niuean uses a compound matua+taane.
Lexical divergence in the word for walk: Tongan reflects PTong *ʔalu, whereas Niuean attests the motion verb haele.

tool_arguments.summary: Reconstruction of Proto-Futunic based on East Futuna and East Uvea. The segmental phonology shows high conservation between the two languages: vowels (*a, *e, *i, *o, *u, and phonemic long vowels *aː, *eː, *oː), glottal stop *ʔ, and consonants *p, *t, *k, *f, *v, *m, *n, *ŋ, *l are retained identically in both daughters. The primary regular consonant divergence is East Futuna s : East Uvea h, reflecting Proto-Futunic *s debuccalized to /h/ in East Uvea (under heavy Tongan contact / areal influence). East Uvea also exhibits a layer of Tongan loanwords (such as nima 'five' with n- for *l-, hui 'bone' for *ivi, and retention of h- in hiŋoa and ʔuhila) as well as an Eastern Polynesian / Tahitian loanword (haːere 'walk' with non-native /r/). Residual affixal and compound material not shared across cognate stems is accounted for under residue_policy 'drop'.

anomalies.explanation: East Uvea haːere is an Eastern Polynesian loanword (most likely via Tahitian missionary contact), evidenced by the phoneme /r/ which is foreign to native East Uvean phonology, contrasting with native East Futuna saʔele (Proto-Polynesian *saʔele).

East Uvea nima exhibits initial /n/ due to borrowing from Tongan numeral nima (where Proto-Polynesian *l shifted to n in numerals), contrasting with East Futuna lima which retains Proto-Polynesian *lima.
East Uvea hui is borrowed from Tongan hui, replacing native Futunic *ivi retained in East Futuna ivi (Proto-Polynesian *iwi).
East Uvea hiŋoa reflects Tongan influence/borrowing retaining initial h-, whereas East Futuna and other Nuclear Polynesian languages regularly lost Proto-Polynesian *h- (iŋoa).
East Uvea ʔuhila exhibits medial -h- influenced by Tongan ʔuhila, whereas East Futuna and Nuclear Polynesian regularly lack -h- (ʔuila).
East Futuna lafu in mu+ŋaː+lafu shows irregular vowel assimilation to /a/ from Proto-Polynesian *refu/*lefu, whereas East Uvea retains original *e in lefu.
East Futuna aːu+sia has suffixation with -sia and root remodeling compared to East Uvea ʔahu (Proto-Polynesian *ʔahu/*ʔasu).
Divergent morphology in 'yawn': East Futuna maːva+va vs East Uvea ma+maːo, showing different suffixation and reduplication patterns on Proto-Polynesian *mawa.

anomalies.explanation: Hawaiian makuakāne reflects compounding of *matua with +kāne ('male'), whereas North Marquesan motua reflects the simplex etymon *matua with sporadic pre-dental vowel rounding.
North Marquesan hoʔolono reflects prefixation with the causative *faka- > hoʔo- onto the base *rono, whereas Hawaiian reflects the simplex lono.
North Marquesan iʔuna preserves the locative prefix *i- fused with *runa, whereas Hawaiian luna reflects the bare root.

North Marquesan vehine shows regressive vowel assimilation/fronting *a > e (*wahine > vehine), in addition to an attested bare root hine.
North Marquesan ʔenata shows irregular initial debuccalization *t > ʔ and vowel fronting *a > e from PPN *taŋata (cf. regular Hawaiian kanaka < *tanata).

tool_arguments.summary: Proto-Marquesic is reconstructed on the basis of regular correspondences between Hawaiian and North Marquesan. Hawaiian underwent backing of *t > k, debuccalization of *k > ʔ and *f > h, merger of *l and *r as l, and shift of *v > w. North Marquesan retained *t, *k, *f, and *v, but debuccalized *r > ʔ (merging with Proto-Polynesian *ʔ). Because each daughter retains phonemic contrasts merged in the other (*t vs *k vs *ʔ, *f vs *h, *r vs *ʔ), the parent Proto-Marquesic inventory is unambiguously reconstructed with consonants *p, *t, *k, *ʔ, *m, *n, *f, *h, *v, *r, and vowels *a, *e, *i, *o, *u, along with phonemic vowel length (*aː, *oː). Regular correspondence sets cover all 46 comparative concepts; remaining unmatched columns stem from morphological discrepancies (affixation with locative *i-, causative *faka-, or compound elements) and sporadic vowel assimilations.

Hawaiian wāwae shows reduplicative or prefixal enlargement wā- on the base *waqe, whereas North Marquesan retains the simplex vae.
North Marquesan vehine shows regressive vowel assimilation/fronting *a > e (*wahine > vehine), in addition to an attested bare root hine.
North Marquesan ʔenata shows irregular initial debuccalization *t > ʔ and vowel fronting *a > e from PPN *taŋata (cf. regular Hawaiian kanaka < *tanata).
